formulas.title: Total Magnification Formula
formulas.eq: Total magnification = objective magnification × eyepiece magnification
formulas.note: This is the single most tested calculation in microscopy: always multiply, never add.

formulas.title: Abbe's Resolution Equation
formulas.worked: Using green light (λ≈550nm) with NA=1.4 gives d ≈ 550/(2×1.4) ≈ 196 nm
formulas.note: Smaller d means better (finer) resolution; shorter wavelength or higher numerical aperture improves resolution.

formulas.title: Actual Specimen Size Calculation
formulas.eq: Actual size = measured size ÷ total magnification (with consistent units)
formulas.worked: An object measuring 4mm under 400x total magnification is actually 4mm/400 = 0.01mm = 10 µm
formulas.note: Always convert to consistent units (usually micrometers) before reporting a final answer.

formulas.title: Field of View Size Estimate
formulas.eq: Field diameter at higher power = (field diameter at lower power × lower power) ÷ higher power
formulas.worked: If low power (100x) field is 1500 µm and you switch to high power (400x): 1500×100/400 = 375 µm
formulas.note: Useful for estimating specimen size or counting cells across different magnifications.

formulas.title: Surface Area to Volume Ratio
formulas.eq: SA:V = surface area ÷ volume (for a cube: 6s² ÷ s³ = 6/s)
formulas.worked: A cube with side 2 µm: SA=6(2²)=24 µm², V=2³=8 µm³, SA:V=3
formulas.note: As a cell grows larger, its SA:V ratio decreases, limiting efficient exchange of nutrients and waste — a key constraint on cell size.

formulas.title: Percent Solute Concentration (Tonicity Setup)
formulas.worked: 5 g of NaCl dissolved to make 100 mL of solution = 5% (w/v) NaCl solution
formulas.note: Comparing this percentage to a cell's internal solute concentration determines whether a solution is hypotonic, isotonic, or hypertonic.

formulas.title: Osmotic Pressure Relationship (van't Hoff-type)
formulas.eq: π = MRT (i included for dissociating solutes: π = iMRT)
formulas.worked: A 0.1 M solution of a non-dissociating solute at 310K: π = (0.1)(0.0821)(310) ≈ 2.55 atm
formulas.note: Higher solute concentration produces greater osmotic pressure, driving more water movement across a membrane.

formulas.title: Centrifugal Force (Relative Centrifugal Force)
formulas.eq: RCF (x g) = 1.118 × 10⁻⁵ × r × N² (r in cm, N in rpm)
formulas.note: Cell fractionation protocols specify RCF (x g), not rpm, because RCF also depends on the rotor's radius.

formulas.title: Cell Doubling Time (Binary Fission)
formulas.eq: N = N₀ × 2ⁿ (n = number of generations elapsed)
formulas.worked: Starting with 1 bacterium and 5 generations (doublings): N = 1 × 2⁵ = 32 cells
formulas.note: Useful for estimating bacterial population growth over a known time period given a constant generation time.

typein.q: What is the refractive index of air, as used in NA calculations?
typein.e: Air has a refractive index of 1.00, the lowest of the media typically compared in microscopy.

typein.q: At 10x magnification, what is the approximate numerical aperture of a Plan Apochromat objective?
typein.e: A Plan Apochromat objective at 10x has an approximate NA of 0.45 — higher than the achromat (0.25) or fluorite (0.30) at the same power, due to its superior aberration correction.

typein.q: On a paper chromatogram, the solvent front travels 10.0 cm from the origin and a pigment spot travels 4.0 cm. What is its Rf value?
typein.e: Rf = distance travelled by the component ÷ distance travelled by the solvent front = 4.0 / 10.0 = 0.40.

cards.q: What is meant by magnification as applied to microscopy?
cards.a: Ratio of the image size formed by the instrument to the actual size of the object
cards.e: Magnification is simply how much bigger the image looks compared with the real object; it says nothing about how clear or well-resolved that bigger image is.

cards.q: How has spherical aberration been overcome in the simple microscope?
cards.a: Fitting a stop/diaphragm that blocks peripheral rays and admits only central rays
cards.e: A simple aperture stop cuts out the marginal rays that a single lens bends too strongly, so only the well-focused central rays reach the eye, correcting spherical aberration.

cards.q: What is the advantage of the oil immersion lens?
cards.a: Oil matches glass's refractive index, cutting ray loss and raising resolving power
cards.e: Without oil, light bends (refracts) as it passes from glass into air, losing rays that carry fine detail; oil matches the refractive index of glass so more rays reach the objective, improving resolution.

cards.q: How has spherical and chromatic aberration been overcome in the modern (compound) microscope?
cards.a: Combining lenses of differing shape and refractive index so their distortions cancel
cards.e: Modern objectives are built from several lens elements of differing curvature and glass type; combined, their individual aberrations cancel out, correcting both spherical and chromatic aberration together.

cards.q: Compound microscopes today can produce 'useful magnification'. How would you explain this to a JSS1 brother starting microscopy?
cards.a: Magnifying only up to the point where more detail still appears, not beyond
cards.e: Useful magnification is magnification matched to the microscope's resolving power — increasing it further than that only enlarges the blur, so it isn't 'useful' anymore.

cards.q: Explain the validity of: 'The diaphragm in part controls magnification.'
cards.a: Invalid — the diaphragm regulates light entering the condenser, not image size
cards.e: Magnification is fixed by the eyepiece and objective lenses in use; the diaphragm only adjusts the amount and angle of light reaching the specimen, so it plays no part in magnification.

cards.q: Explain the validity of: 'The diaphragm in part controls contrast.'
cards.a: Valid — narrowing it cuts stray light, raising specimen-to-background contrast
cards.e: Closing the iris diaphragm cuts down scattered light and increases the contrast of the image, which is the main everyday use of the diaphragm control on a light microscope.

cards.q: Explain the validity of: 'The diaphragm in part controls resolution.'
cards.a: Valid — closing it too far shrinks the aperture and lowers resolving power
cards.e: The diaphragm sets the cone angle (numerical aperture) of light entering the condenser; closing it too much shrinks that angle and reduces the resolving power, even while raising contrast.

cards.q: The limit of resolution of two optical instruments is (a) 5 nm and (b) 5 µm. Which has the better resolving power?
cards.a: Instrument (a), since a smaller limit of resolution means finer detail is resolved
cards.e: Resolving power is better when the limit of resolution is smaller — 5 nm (0.005 µm) is a thousand times finer than 5 µm, so instrument (a) resolves far finer detail.

cards.q: In what ways can contrast be improved in a specimen?
cards.a: Staining, narrowing the diaphragm, or using dark-field/phase-contrast/fluorescence
cards.e: Contrast is raised by making structures absorb or scatter light differently from their background — staining and diaphragm control do this directly, and dark-field/phase-contrast/fluorescence are built specifically to enhance contrast in unstained material.

cards.q: What makes biological specimens appear too light, giving very poor contrast when viewed unstained?
cards.a: Mostly transparent and watery, so they absorb little light and barely differ from the background
cards.e: Living cells are largely water and thin, nearly colourless material, so light passes through with little absorption, leaving almost no brightness difference between specimen and background — hence poor contrast.

cards.q: A microbiologist wants to view an unstained microbial cell. Should bright-field or dark-field be used, and why?
cards.a: Dark-field, since it shows the transparent cell bright against a dark background, raising contrast
cards.e: Unstained microbial cells are nearly transparent and give poor contrast in bright-field; dark-field illuminates them with oblique light only, so they scatter light and glow brightly against a dark background.

cards.q: What modification converts a bright-field microscope into a dark-field microscope?
cards.a: An opaque central stop is fitted in the condenser, so only oblique rays reach the specimen
cards.e: Blocking the central light path with a special stop leaves only scattered, oblique light hitting the specimen; only light diffracted by the specimen itself reaches the objective, so the field appears dark except where the specimen scatters light.

cards.q: What modification converts a bright-field microscope into a phase-contrast microscope?
cards.a: An annular diaphragm and matching phase plate turn phase shifts into brightness
cards.e: Phase-contrast optics use a ring-shaped (annular) diaphragm and a matching phase plate in the objective that shift and recombine diffracted and undiffracted light, turning the invisible phase shifts caused by the specimen into visible contrast.

cards.q: Explain the validity of: 'The phase-contrast microscope increases magnification.'
cards.a: Invalid — it changes how contrast is produced, not the lenses' magnifying power
cards.e: Phase-contrast is purely a contrast-enhancing technique; the magnifying power still comes entirely from the ordinary objective and eyepiece lenses used.

cards.q: Explain the validity of: 'The phase-contrast microscope increases contrast.'
cards.a: Valid — it converts invisible phase shifts in the light into visible brightness differences
cards.e: This is the whole purpose of the technique: it lets unstained, living, transparent cells be seen clearly by turning their subtle phase-shifting effect on light into visible contrast.

cards.q: Explain the validity of: 'The phase-contrast microscope improves resolution.'
cards.a: Invalid — resolving power still depends on wavelength and numerical aperture, unchanged
cards.e: Phase-contrast changes how contrast is generated, but the resolving power of the microscope is still governed by the same wavelength and numerical-aperture limits as any light microscope.

cards.q: How does the amplitude of the light used relate to the contrast of a specimen?
cards.a: A bigger amplitude difference between specimen and background is seen as greater contrast
cards.e: Amplitude of a light wave corresponds to its intensity, which the eye perceives as brightness; the larger the amplitude difference between specimen and background, the more contrast is seen.

cards.q: How does the wavelength of the light used relate to the contrast of a specimen?
cards.a: Structures absorb different wavelengths unequally, so chosen colours/filters can raise contrast
cards.e: Wavelength determines colour, and specimen structures absorb different colours to different degrees, so choosing or filtering wavelength (as with stains or colour filters) can bring out contrast between structures.

cards.q: In phase-contrast microscopy, retardation of diffracted rays relative to undiffracted rays depends on specimen thickness and density. Explain how these influence the image.
cards.a: Thicker/denser regions retard light more, so the phase plate renders them with stronger brightness contrast
cards.e: A greater optical path length (more thickness or higher refractive index/density) produces a larger phase shift in the diffracted light, which the phase plate turns into a correspondingly larger brightness difference — more contrast for denser or thicker parts.

cards.q: Light of shorter wavelength is converted into light of longer wavelength in fluorescence microscopy. Explain how this is possible.
cards.a: A fluorochrome absorbs short-wavelength light and re-emits it, after an energy loss, at a longer wavelength
cards.e: Fluorescence works because an excited electron in the fluorochrome loses a little energy internally before it drops back down and emits a photon; since energy and wavelength are inversely related, the emitted photon has lower energy and therefore a longer wavelength than the light that excited it.

cards.q: Explain the function of the second barrier filter in UV/fluorescence microscopy.
cards.a: It blocks leftover excitation light, passing only the emitted fluorescent light through
cards.e: Without a barrier filter, harmful/bright excitation light would swamp the much dimmer fluorescence signal and could damage the eye; the second barrier filter removes the excitation wavelengths so only the emitted fluorescence is seen.

cards.q: Explain why the electron microscope is used to observe only dead specimens.
cards.a: Because the specimen needs a vacuum and is fixed, dehydrated and often metal-coated, which kills it
cards.e: Electron microscopy requires a vacuum (electrons are absorbed by air) plus fixation, dehydration and often metal coating of the specimen — conditions that are lethal, so only dead, processed specimens can be viewed.

cards.q: 'The UV/fluorescence microscope cannot be used to view dead specimens.' Explain the truth or otherwise of this statement.
cards.a: Fluorescence depends on the dye used, not on the cell being alive, so dead specimens work too
cards.e: Fluorescence is a property of the fluorochrome reacting to excitation light, not of cell metabolism, so fixed/dead, stained tissue is routinely and successfully examined by fluorescence microscopy.

cards.q: Why does the electron microscope provide so much more resolution than the light microscope?
cards.a: Because electrons have a far shorter wavelength, and resolving power improves as wavelength shortens
cards.e: The limit of resolution is proportional to the wavelength of the imaging radiation; the wavelength associated with an accelerated electron beam is thousands of times shorter than visible light, giving vastly better resolution.

cards.q: In dehydration and embedding for light microscopy, alcohol, xylene and paraffin wax are used. What property of xylene makes it suitable here?
cards.a: Xylene mixes with both alcohol and molten wax, clearing the alcohol so wax can infiltrate
cards.e: Xylene dissolves in alcohol and also in melted paraffin wax, so it 'clears' the alcohol out of the dehydrated tissue and lets the wax move in — which is exactly why this clearing step sits between dehydration and wax infiltration.

cards.q: In order to cut ultra-thin sections of a biological specimen, what should be the nature of the embedding medium?
cards.a: Very hard and rigid, so extremely thin sections can be cut without tearing
cards.e: Ultra-thin sections (as needed for electron microscopy) require a hard, rigid resin embedding, since a soft medium like paraffin wax would crumple or tear rather than allow such extremely thin, clean cuts.

cards.q: Why are lysosomes referred to as 'suicide bags'?
cards.a: Escaped digestive enzymes from a ruptured lysosome can destroy the whole cell
cards.e: Lysosomal enzymes can digest proteins, lipids and nucleic acids; if the lysosomal membrane ruptures and these enzymes escape into the cytoplasm, they can digest the cell itself — hence the nickname 'suicide bags'.

cards.q: Why are lysosomes more predominant in phagocytic cells than in non-phagocytic cells?
cards.a: Phagocytic cells digest engulfed pathogens, needing many lysosomal enzymes to do so
cards.e: Phagocytosis involves engulfing particles/microbes into vesicles that must be broken down; lysosomes supply the enzymes for this, so cells specialised for phagocytosis carry far more of them than cells that don't engulf material.
